questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features that mark a totalitarian project.
questions.stem: In an intake note, a patient describes a state that claims one doctrine explains all of society and seeks to reach every part of life. Which feature does this describe?

options.text: An ideology claiming comprehensive reach, pursued through a state party
A state that allows many competing parties to contest elections regularly
options.misconception: describes competitive pluralism, which contradicts totalitarianism

options.text: A state where political life is simply one area among many others
options.misconception: confuses a pluralistic state with a totalitarian one

options.text: A state that leaves economic management to private owners and farmers
options.misconception: reads economic liberalisation as a mark of totalitarian ideology

questions.explanation: Totalitarianism rests on an ideology claiming to explain society as a whole and seeks to organise every domain of life, typically through a party that embodies it. Competitive elections and a limited political sphere are its opposites.
questions.hint: Ask how far the doctrine claims to reach.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a regime from a clinical intake account.

stimulus.body: History: patient is a former municipal clerk, now working as a shop assistant. Notes: states that elections are held on a fixed schedule and that a majority party does hold office. Patient reports that the party's opponents are permitted to contest seats and that some opposition mayors govern their towns, though no-one who won a recent by-election against the governing party has been allowed to take office. Also reports that the national television channel broadcasts official statements without comment.

questions.stem: On the basis of the intake note, how should this political setting be classified?

options.text: A democratic system, because elections are held on a regular schedule
options.misconception: treats regular elections alone as sufficient for a democratic classification

options.text: A hybrid regime, since elections occur but competitive results are not respected
An authoritarian regime, because opposition candidates are prevented from taking office
options.misconception: ignores the parts of the note that show competitive pluralism still operating

options.text: A totalitarian regime, because the state controls what is broadcast nationally
options.misconception: infers totalitarianism from control of broadcasting without an ideology

questions.explanation: The note combines real pluralism, contested seats and opposition mayors, with the blocking of a result the governing party lost, which fits a hybrid regime. Broadcasting control alone says nothing about totalitarianism.
questions.hint: Ask whether the winner of a contest is allowed to govern.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain democratic deficit as a shortfall in quality.
questions.stem: Explain what democratic deficit means in a clinician's assessment of a country's political system, and why the concept is about quality rather than the presence of elections.

answer.exemplar: Democratic deficit describes the gap between the institutions a country formally has and the standards those institutions are meant to meet, such as meaningful accountability, genuine competition, the rule of law and the respect for rights. A country can hold elections regularly and still show a large deficit if results are not respected, if courts are not independent, or if the media cannot question those in power. The concept is therefore about quality: it asks how well the system performs against democratic standards, not whether a democratic feature exists in name.

questions.explanation: Democratic deficit is the shortfall between formal institutions and democratic standards such as accountability, competition and the rule of law. It concerns quality of performance, not whether elections exist on paper.
questions.hint: Ask how well the system performs, not whether it exists.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the minimal and maximal definitions to a patient's account.

stimulus.body: Note: during a follow-up the patient says that in her country people can change the government by voting, and that officials can be removed from office if they break the law. Asked whether the state guarantees freedom of speech, she hesitates and says she is not sure what the rules provide.

options.text: The maximal definition is not established, since she cannot confirm the free speech guarantee
Neither definition applies, since she describes competitive elections in a stable state
options.misconception: treats a partly descriptive account as excluding every definition

questions.explanation: The account confirms minimal features, electoral change and removal of officials by law, while leaving the maximal requirement of guaranteed free speech unestablished. Her uncertainty is not confirmation.
questions.hint: Separate what she confirmed from what she did not.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh a democratic claim against counter-evidence in a survey note.

stimulus.body: A district health survey asked residents whether the last national election was free and fair. Overall, 58 per cent said yes, 29 per cent said no and 13 per cent did not know. questions.stem: Given the note, how should a claim that the elections were democratic be assessed?

options.text: The claim should be accepted, because a majority of residents confirm the elections were free
options.misconception: treats a bare majority of respondents as settling the question of fairness

options.text: The claim needs scrutiny, since the lowest confirmation coincides with documented intimidation
The claim should be rejected outright, because no district reports a majority of confidence
options.misconception: jumps to rejection without testing the claim against the evidence

questions.explanation: A majority statement that the elections were free is weakest where intimidation is documented, so the claim needs scrutiny rather than acceptance or automatic rejection. Variation across districts is informative.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare the reach of socialising agents across regime types.
questions.stem: Explain how the reach of socialising agents differs under a totalitarian regime compared with a liberal democracy, and state one practical consequence for citizens.

answer.exemplar: In a liberal democracy the socialising agents are plural and each reaches only part of the population, so the family, schools, the media and the workplace pull in different directions and no single source can reach everyone. Under totalitarianism the party state aims to occupy the same spaces, so the family, the school, the workplace and the media are all organised to deliver the official line, and the reach of the official message is far greater. For citizens this means the practical room for forming an independent view is much narrower, and private groups cannot assume that school or work will offer any protection for dissent.

questions.explanation: Plural agents each reach part of the population in a liberal democracy, while a totalitarian state seeks to occupy every space and deliver one message. The consequence is a far narrower scope for forming an independent view.
questions.hint: Ask how much of life the official message can enter.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why democracy is measured along four dimensions.
questions.stem: Explain why democracy is measured along four dimensions rather than by a single indicator, and give one reason each dimension can fail on its own.

answer.exemplar: The four dimensions capture distinct requirements. Participation can be wide while competition is narrow, if elections are held in a one-party market, and the reverse is possible if seats are contested in a system where the vote does not translate into seats. Vertical accountability can be formal while expression is restricted, if a constitution prescribes courts and a legislature that the government ignores. Freedom of expression can be broad while accountability is broken, if criticism is tolerated in the press but no body can call officials to account. A single indicator would let a failure in one dimension pass unnoticed behind strength in another.

questions.explanation: Each dimension can fail while the others hold, so a single indicator lets strengths conceal weaknesses. Free elections do not guarantee free expression, and wide participation does not guarantee that outcomes are respected.
questions.hint: One dimension can fail while others hold.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why hybrid regimes are hard to classify yet useful.
questions.stem: Explain why hybrid regimes are difficult to classify and why analysts nevertheless find the category useful.

answer.exemplar: A hybrid regime mixes competitive and authoritarian features, so any single test produces a misleading result: elections may be held regularly while the loser cannot take office, a constitution may be respected while the courts are packed, and a parliament may sit while the executive rules by decree. The features pull in opposite directions, and the balance changes over time and across regions, which is why pure labels often mislead. The category is useful because it captures what the extremes miss, and because it invites the analyst to examine which features are present rather than to assume that one decisive test exists.

questions.explanation: Hybrid regimes combine competitive and authoritarian features, so a single test misleads and the balance shifts over time and across regions. The category is useful because it directs attention to which features are actually present.
questions.hint: Ask which features are present, not which label fits.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A democratic claim and its counter-evidence
questions.learningObjective: Set out the kinds of counter-evidence that defeat a democratic claim.
questions.stem: Set out the kinds of counter-evidence that would most weaken a government's claim to be a democracy, and explain why each matters.

answer.exemplar: Three kinds of counter-evidence are decisive. First, systematic distortion of the electoral process, such as votes not counting equally, systematic disqualification of candidates, or results not respected, undermines the claim that the government derives its authority from the people. Second, suppression of contestation, shown by bans on parties and journalists, tells the same story about the possibility of replacement. Third, failure of accountability, where courts and legislatures cannot call officials to account, indicates that elections cannot discipline power even if they are competitive. Each bears on a different part of the claim, which is why a single favourable indicator cannot sustain it.

questions.explanation: Distortion of the electoral process, suppression of contestation and failure of accountability each attack a different part of the democratic claim. A single favourable indicator therefore cannot sustain the claim on its own.
questions.hint: Test the claim at elections, contestation and accountability.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two definitions circulate and what choosing one implies.
questions.stem: Explain why two definitions of democracy circulate in political analysis, and state the practical consequence of choosing one.

answer.exemplar: The minimal definition, centred on elected government and the rule of law, is easy to apply and gives comparable results across large numbers of countries. The maximal definition, which adds free expression, strong opposition and active participation, describes democracy as a fuller way of life. Both are used because each suits a different purpose: the minimal one for broad comparative measurement, the maximal one for judging whether a system sustains the conditions of political freedom. The practical consequence is that the same country can be counted democratic under one and not the other, so any claim about how many democracies exist depends on the definition stated.

questions.explanation: The minimal definition supports broad comparison, while the maximal one judges the fuller conditions of political freedom. The choice changes which countries count as democracies, so the definition must be stated.
questions.hint: Ask what a classification depends on the choice.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the organisational and ideological pursuit of a totalitarian project.
questions.stem: Explain how the reach of an ideology distinguishes a totalitarian project from ordinary party competition, and give two ways the project is pursued.

answer.exemplar: Ordinary party competition involves persuading voters and forming governments within institutions that already exist. A totalitarian project instead claims to hold the whole of society together and seeks to remake the institutions that would otherwise constrain it. Two ways it is pursued are organisational, as a party state that supplies every service and places officials in every workplace, school and neighbourhood, and ideological, as a doctrine presented as a complete account of history and society so that disagreement appears as error or pathology rather than as politics. The first makes the message unavoidable and the second makes it hard to argue with.

questions.explanation: Party competition seeks votes within existing institutions, while a totalitarian project claims the whole of society and remakes the institutions that would constrain it. It is pursued organisationally, through a party state in every setting, and ideologically, through a doctrine treated as complete truth.
questions.hint: Ask whether the message aims to cover all of life.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Reading a regime from its features
questions.learningObjective: Describe a defensible method for reading regime features.
questions.stem: Explain how an analyst should read a profile of regime features so that the classification is defensible rather than impressionistic.

answer.exemplar: A defensible reading works through the features systematically. It checks whether competitive elections are held, whether the results are respected, whether opposition parties and independent media can operate, whether courts and legislatures can hold the executive to account, and whether rights are limited in practice. It then asks which features are present, which are absent and which are only formally present, and it looks for the pattern rather than a single indicator, because regimes differ in degree and in the balance between features. It also records what the evidence cannot settle, and separates description from classification.

questions.explanation: A defensible reading checks elections, results, opposition, media, accountability and rights, then weighs which features are present, absent or merely formal. It works from a pattern rather than a single indicator and separates description from classification.
questions.hint: Work through the features, then weigh the pattern.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare two countries using dimension-by-dimension deficit.
questions.stem: Explain how the idea of democratic deficit can be used to compare a country with strong elections and weak accountability against one with weaker elections and stronger accountability.

answer.exemplar: The comparison shows why the concept is needed rather than a simple pass or fail label. The first country may have competitive elections and a high turnout, which satisfies the minimal definition, but if the executive cannot be questioned effectively the standards of accountability are unmet. The second may have less competitive elections, yet a legislature that regularly holds the government to account and a press that is free to criticise it meet other standards. Deficit is therefore assessed dimension by dimension, so the two countries may show different shortfalls rather than a single ranking, and the comparison rests on the standards stated rather than on an overall impression.

questions.explanation: Because deficit is assessed dimension by dimension, a country with strong elections but weak accountability and one with weaker elections but stronger accountability show different shortfalls rather than a single ranking. The comparison rests on stated standards.
questions.hint: Compare dimension by dimension, not in the abstract.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how agent reach shapes what citizens can learn.
questions.stem: Explain how the reach of socialising agents affects what a citizen can learn about politics, and why this matters for judging a regime's openness.

answer.exemplar: Where many agents operate and can be reached, a citizen meets competing accounts of what is happening, and can compare them, weigh them and draw conclusions that no single source intended. Where one agent reaches nearly every setting, the citizen is repeatedly given the same account, presented through institutions that carry authority, so independent judgement has little raw material to work on. This matters for judging openness because the reach of socialising agents is what turns a formal permission to speak into an effective chance to hear competing views, and it is therefore an informal constraint on political pluralism.

questions.explanation: Plural agents give citizens material for comparison and judgement, while a single pervasive agent leaves little to weigh independently. Reach therefore turns formal permission to speak into an effective chance to hear competing views.
questions.hint: Ask what a citizen has available to compare.

options.misconception: confuses the presence of institutions with effective democratic practice

options.text: A deficit located entirely in the institutions the note names
options.misconception: misplaces the shortfall inside institutions that the note says work

options.text: A deficit caused by the design of the electoral commission
options.misconception: attributes the shortfall to one body's design without evidence

questions.explanation: The institutions are present and working, so the shortfall lies in how little the government is questioned and how narrow public debate is, concerning participation and accountability rather than institutional design.
questions.hint: Look at practice rather than at the written design.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read uneven access to influence in a clinical account.

stimulus.body: Note: patient says her country has a freely elected parliament, that the courts can rule against the government and that people may criticise it in print. She says her own brother is a member of the ruling party and can get any local official on the telephone, while a group of neighbours who posted a critical letter were visited by officials within a day. She concludes that in her country everyone has an opinion but only some can act on it.

questions.stem: Which reading of the patient's account is best supported?

options.text: Neither standard is met, because the closing of the local group invalidates the elections
options.misconception: invalidates the electoral standard on the basis of one incident

options.text: The minimal standard is met, and the maximal one fails on uneven access to influence
Both standards are met, since criticism in print is legally permitted
options.misconception: treats legal permission as proof that the maximal standard is satisfied

options.text: The note proves that the patient's family holds disproportionate political influence
options.misconception: draws a class conclusion that the note does not license

questions.explanation: An elected parliament and courts that can rule against the government meet the minimal definition, but access to attention varies sharply with connections, as the patient's family shows. Legal permission to criticise does not make influence even.
questions.hint: Ask who can turn an opinion into action.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Use the dimensions as a diagnostic for classification.
questions.stem: Explain how the four dimensions of democracy can be used as a diagnostic when a country's overall classification seems obvious.

answer.exemplar: A classification can hide more than it reveals when a country is called democratic on the strength of elections alone, so the dimensions give an analyst a way to locate the actual weakness. Participation may be numerically high yet shaped by pressure rather than choice; competition may be formally open while the effective number of viable parties is one; vertical accountability may exist on paper while officials evade scrutiny through procedural delay; and expression may be tolerated in private while the media that could carry it are owned by the government. Working through each dimension shows which commitment is real and which is only stated, and it also prevents a strong dimension from being used to excuse a weak one.

questions.explanation: Working through each dimension shows which commitment is real and which is merely stated, and it stops a strong dimension from excusing a weak one. A single overall label would conceal where the shortfall actually lies.
questions.hint: Use the dimensions to locate the weak point.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Reading a regime from its features
questions.learningObjective: Identify party-state reach through the school classroom.

stimulus.body: Note: patient, a retired local teacher, describes a country where teachers are required to deliver approved lessons, where the education ministry inspects classrooms each term, and where a text on the history of the country used in schools presents the previous period as a period of national humiliation caused by enemies. She adds that she no longer teaches history because the lessons became politically contested in the staff room.

questions.stem: Reading the note, which feature of the regime does the classroom most clearly reveal?

options.text: A liberal regime in which teachers are free to disagree with the ministry
options.misconception: reads enforced approved lessons as evidence of freedom to disagree

options.text: A hybrid regime in which education policy alternates with changes of government
options.misconception: invents alternation in education policy that the note does not mention

options.text: The party state reaching into education to deliver an approved account of the past
A totalitarian regime in which every subject is taught from a single approved text
options.misconception: infers totalitarianism from one subject being taught from approved material

questions.explanation: Approved lessons, term-time inspection and a single authorised account of the national past show the state directing education and the official view of history, which is party-state reach into a key setting. One subject does not establish totalitarianism.
questions.hint: Ask who decides what is taught.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A democratic claim and its counter-evidence
questions.learningObjective: Assess a democratic claim resting on electoral features alone.
questions.stem: Which assessment best fits a government's claim of democracy that rests on regular elections, published results and competitive parties?

options.text: The claim must be accepted, because competitive parties and published results are decisive
options.misconception: accepts institutional evidence as conclusive without testing the rest

options.text: The claim must be rejected, because no country meets every democratic standard fully
options.misconception: applies an absolute standard that would disqualify every country

options.text: The claim is unassessable, because democratic standards vary between countries
options.misconception: declines to assess the claim at all because standards differ

options.text: The claim needs further evidence on accountability and rights before it holds

questions.explanation: Regular elections, published results and competitive parties meet minimal standards, but a claim to democracy needs evidence about accountability, rights and the treatment of opponents. Standards may be debated without abandoning assessment.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim has not yet shown.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise informal groups as socialising settings.
questions.stem: A community clinic runs a weekly discussion group that many residents attend. What does this show about the reach of socialising agents?

options.text: Voluntary groups are a setting in which views are formed and exchanged outside family and school
Only the family and the school can socialise citizens politically at all
options.misconception: confines socialising agents to the family and the school

options.text: Attending a discussion group guarantees that its speakers are believed
options.misconception: assumes attendance implies acceptance of what is said

options.text: Informal groups always transmit official political messages better than families do
options.misconception: presumes informal groups are better transmitters of official messages

questions.explanation: Discussion groups create a setting where residents form and exchange views outside the family and the classroom, extending the reach of socialising influence. Attendance implies no agreement, and such groups usually carry independent messages.
questions.hint: Ask what happens in settings beyond the household.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a combination of totalitarian features.

stimulus.body: Note: patient describes a state where the party keeps files on every citizen's political activity, where the state controls the labour market so that party membership affects employment, where organisations other than the party are dissolved if they are judged insufficiently loyal, and where the party's leader is presented in public as the embodiment of the nation's historical destiny.

questions.stem: According to the note, which combination of features is present?

options.text: Administrative monitoring, economic control and doctrinal leadership combined in one party
Competitive elections alongside a strong tradition of civil liberties
options.misconception: treats party control of files and jobs as ordinary administrative practice

options.text: A federal structure balancing regional and central authority carefully
options.misconception: invents a federal arrangement the note never mentions

options.text: A planned economy with no political party involved in economic decisions
options.misconception: assumes the absence of a plan means the absence of party involvement

questions.explanation: Files on political activity, party membership affecting employment and the dissolution of organisations show the party present in administration, the economy and civil life, while the leader is cast as national destiny. This is totalitarian reach.
questions.hint: Ask how many parts of life the party enters.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a hybrid regime from an illiberal democracy.
questions.stem: Explain how a researcher might distinguish a hybrid regime from a democracy that is merely illiberal, and why the distinction is worth drawing.

answer.exemplar: An illiberal democracy remains a democracy on the central test: leaders are chosen by competitive elections that decide who governs, and the results are respected, even if rights are restricted in practice and courts are weak. A hybrid regime retains those competitive forms while also embedding features that prevent a genuine contest, such as a state that decides the count, disqualifies opponents or dismisses elected governments. The distinction matters because the remedies differ: an illiberal democracy needs judicial independence and rights protections, whereas a hybrid regime needs the electoral process itself restored before its other features can be assessed.

questions.explanation: An illiberal democracy still decides who governs through competitive elections whose results are respected, while a hybrid regime retains those forms while preventing a real contest. The distinction matters because the remedies differ.
questions.hint: Ask whether the election decides who governs.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess a democratic deficit from a retired teacher's account.

stimulus.body: Note: patient, a retired teacher, reports that in her country a legislative assembly is elected every four years, that all major parties are represented in it, that debates are televised, and that the assembly has twice rejected a government bill. She also notes that the electoral commission is appointed by the governing party and that the only television channels broadcast its statements without reply from opponents.

questions.stem: Given the note, which assessment of the democratic deficit is most accurate?

options.text: A deficit exists, arising from electoral management and one-sided broadcasting
options.misconception: confuses the presence of plural institutions with an absence of deficit

options.text: No deficit exists, because elections, televised debate and a rejecting assembly are present
options.misconception: treats democratic features as proof that the standards are all met

options.text: A substantial deficit exists, centred on control of elections and of public broadcasting
A deficit exists only because the assembly rejected two government bills
options.misconception: misreads ordinary legislative disagreement as evidence of democratic failure

questions.explanation: Competitive elections, televised debate and an assembly that rejects bills show genuine pluralism, but a party-appointed electoral commission and one-sided broadcasting leave electoral management and expression deficient. Legislative disagreement is a working check, not a failure.
questions.hint: Look at who controls the count and the airwaves.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State what the two definitions contribute to classification.
questions.stem: Which statement best captures what the two definitions of democracy contribute to a classification exercise?

options.text: They guarantee the same countries are counted democratic under either definition
options.misconception: assumes the two definitions agree on every case

options.text: They remove the need to state which definition the researcher applied
options.misconception: suggests the choice of definition can be left unstated

options.text: They provide a single decisive test for whether a regime is democratic
options.misconception: treats competing definitions as if they resolved into one test

options.text: They let a researcher state clearly what counts as democratic and compare cases

questions.explanation: The two definitions let a researcher state the standard being applied and compare cases against it, which makes a classification defensible. They do not collapse into one test, and the choice cannot be left unstated.
questions.hint: Ask what stating a definition makes possible.
